cards.title: Positioning Is About the Prospect's Mind, Not Your Product
cards.summary: Positioning means manipulating what already exists in the customer's mind—the product ladder—rather than inventing something new.
cards.use_when: Choosing a market position, category entry angle, or brand claim for a store or product line before writing any PDP or ad copy.
steps: Accept the source's core premise: the mind already holds a mental ladder for each category, with brands ranked in it. You cannot argue your way onto a rung the prospect hasn't already reserved space for—you can only take a position that fits an existing hole.
Map the ladder for your category: list the brands a typical customer would name unprompted, in order. This is the ladder you are actually competing on, not your internal product roadmap.
Find the open 'creneau'—a niche or hole in perception. Common creneau types named by the source: size (large or small), high price, low price, age/cohort, time of day, and distribution channel.

Pick a position that fits the hole and that you can credibly defend. Positioning is a perception game, not a product-invention game; a genuinely new feature still needs to correspond to a slot in the mind.
Write PDP headlines, brand claims and ad angles that reinforce the chosen rung consistently, since repetition is what fixes a position in memory.
Re-check the ladder periodically: if a competitor has already claimed the hole, re-position rather than overlap.
caveats: The framework assumes a category already has a leader and a ladder. For a genuinely new category with no occupants, the rules change (see card on coined names).

The book's examples are largely classic consumer brands; the ladder idea transfers to online stores but the specific ladder contents are category- and audience-specific and must be researched, not assumed.

cards.title: The 'Against' Position: How to Be No. 2
cards.summary: If you are not the leader, position against the leader rather than pretending to be one, as Avis did against Hertz.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition creative, brand taglines or comparison landing pages for a store or product that is not the market leader.
steps: Identify the clear category leader in your niche. If you are not first, do not run creative that implies you are; prospects already know who the leader is and will discount the claim.

Adopt the source's 'against' stance: openly acknowledge the leader's position and define yourself in relation to it. The Avis/Hertz example is the model—'we're number two, so we try harder' works because it is true and it earns the prospect's respect.
Turn the leader's strength into the reason you exist for a distinct segment: if the leader is for everyone, position as the specialist; if the leader is cheap, position on quality or service.
If no leader exists in a niche, be the first to occupy it and say so explicitly, rather than relating to a leader who does not exist.
Carry the against-position through your about page, ad copy and PDP claims so the rung is reinforced consistently across touchpoints.
caveats: This is the book's recommended strategy for the No. 2 brand, not a universal rule; a brand with a genuinely novel category can take the 'first' position instead.
An 'against' position depends on the leader being well-known to the prospect. If your audience does not know the leader, the comparison wastes the ad spend.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Uncola Move: Positioning by What You Are Not
cards.summary: Define your brand by the category norm you reject, the way 7-Up positioned as the 'Uncola' rather than as a cola variant.
cards.use_when: Differentiating a product in a crowded category where every competitor claims the same attributes—beverages, supplements, apparel, software.
steps: Identify the dominant convention or attribute in your category that every competitor claims (for cola: cola taste, brown color, the 'cola' identity itself).
Decide whether you can credibly claim the opposite or a distinct alternative that the leader cannot follow without abandoning its own position.
Build the position around exclusion: state what you are not. The source's Uncola example is a soft drink that refused to be a cola and instead owned the non-cola slot.
Apply this to a store: if every rival PDP leads with 'premium materials,' test a position built on what you deliberately omit (no subscription lock-in, no middlemen, no artificial additives).
Keep the negative claim honest and verifiable — it survives scrutiny only if the omission is real.
Reinforce the 'not' position in ad creative, packaging copy and the first above-the-fold line on the PDP.
caveats: The Uncola worked partly because the cola category was enormous and clearly defined; a small or fragmented category may offer no dominant convention to reject.
Negative positioning can read as gimmicky if the underlying product does not deliver a real alternative, so it must match the actual product.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Repositioning the Competition: Undermining the Leader's Concept
cards.summary: Attack the concept the leader owns, not the leader's product, the way Tylenol repositioned aspirin by questioning the stomach-bleeding side effect.
cards.use_when: Planning comparative ad campaigns, review-content angles or landing pages where you need to shift the prospect's view of the incumbent rather than out-shout it.
steps: Identify the single concept the leader owns (aspirin owned 'pain relief'; Tylenol's move was to reframe the conversation around side effects).
Locate a genuine weakness or assumption inside that concept that the leader cannot fix without contradicting its own position.
Reframe the category around that weakness so the prospect re-evaluates the leader on your terms. The source frames this as repositioning the competition by undermining its core idea.
Build your claim on the reframed axis, not on a head-to-head attribute list where the leader's scale wins.
Use comparison and review pages, earned media angles and ad copy consistent with the new axis so the reframe reaches prospects who never saw your ad.

Track whether the reframe is being adopted in customer language; if prospects start using your framing unprompted, the reposition is taking hold. Source-based examples are illustrations, not guaranteed results.
caveats: This is the book's most aggressive tactic and depends on a real, defensible weakness—an invented or exaggerated one invites legal and reputational risk, especially in regulated categories like health.
Attacking a leader's concept may invite a direct response and price war; weigh whether your brand is equipped to sustain that.

cards.title: Factory Creneau vs. Mind Creneau
cards.summary: A gap in your product line is not the same as a gap in the customer's perception; only the latter is a real positioning opportunity.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new SKU, sub-brand or category entry, especially when the gap is obvious on a spreadsheet.
steps: List candidate holes you have identified: missing price tiers, missing sizes, missing formats, missing use cases.

For each, ask whether it exists as a hole in the customer's mind or only in your product line. A factory creneau is a hole in the line; a mind creneau is an actual opening in the prospect's perception, per the source's distinction.
Screen out factory creneaus: a price gap between $30 and $50 in a market where customers only think in '$30-ish' and '$100-ish' is not a position, just an empty shelf.
Prioritize mind creneaus, where prospects already feel a category is missing something or where no brand occupies a distinct concept.
Verify with customer language (search terms, reviews, support tickets) that the gap is felt, not merely visible to your merchandising team.
Only then decide the naming and brand architecture for the new entry, using the house-name vs. new-name rules.
caveats: The book's distinction is conceptual; verifying a mind creneau requires your own customer research, which the source does not specify for ecommerce.
A mind creneau can close quickly if a competitor arrives; speed and reinforcement matter.

cards.title: The Initials Trap: When Abbreviations Dilute Your Brand
cards.summary: Initials and acronyms as brand names only work after a brand is already famous; using them earlier throws away the memory value of a real name.
cards.use_when: Naming or renaming a store, private-label line or sub-brand and choosing between a descriptive/coined name and a set of initials.
steps: Recognize the no-name trap: the source's claim is that initials only work after a brand is already famous because the full name has been burned into memory first. IBM and GE earned their abbreviations; they did not start there.
For a new brand, avoid leading with initials. Use a name that carries phonetic or semantic weight so the prospect has something to hold onto.
A useful check: if the name is an acronym, ask whether the mind holds the underlying words. If not, the initials are only a string of letters with no hook.

If corporate structure forces initials (legal entity, registry constraint), pair the trading name with a memorable, pronounceable brand name on packaging, PDP and ads, treating the initials as back-office only.
For sub-brands, prefer a short, sayable house name over letter strings; test by reading the name aloud in a 3-second ad.
caveats: This is the source's strong opinion about naming, drawn from pre-internet advertising; modern search and logo-led brands sometimes succeed with coined or short names, but the memory argument still favors pronounceable, meaningful names for new entries.
Initials can be useful in domains or handles for consistency; the trap concerns using them as the primary brand expression.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Coined Names: The One Condition for Using Them
cards.summary: A coined name is acceptable only when you are first in the mind with an absolutely new product.
cards.use_when: Choosing a brand name for a genuinely new product category, new store concept or novel private label, rather than a new SKU in an existing category.
steps: Ask the gate question from the source: are you first in the mind with an absolutely new product? If yes, a coined name may work because there is no existing ladder to fight against and the name can define the category.
If the answer is no—if the category already has occupants—a coined name forces you to spend extra advertising to teach the prospect what the word means before you can position anything.
For most catalog additions, favor descriptive or suggestive names: they carry meaning into the mind at zero teaching cost.
If you do coin a name, make it short, pronounceable, and reinforce it with an explicit category descriptor in the same ad or PDP headline until the name alone evokes the category.
Consider negative or unusual names cautiously: the source notes negative names can attract attention, but attention alone is not a position.
Revisit the name decision if the category later fills up—being first is what justified the coined name in the first place.
caveats: The source's rule is strict: coined names are only sanctioned for first-in-mind novel products. Applying them to ordinary new SKUs is the failure mode this rule guards against.
Category-first status can be lost; the coined-name advantage is not permanent.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The 5 Rules of the Road for House Name vs. New Name
cards.summary: Use five criteria—volume, competition, ad support, significance and distribution—to decide whether a new product rides the house name or gets its own.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand architecture for a line extension: whether a new SKU, category or sub-brand should carry the house brand or a separate name.
steps: Rule 1 — Expected volume: a large expected volume can justify a new name; small volume favours riding the existing house brand where recognition is already paid for.
Rule 2 — Competition: with strong, established competitors, a distinct new name may help carve out a position; in a fragmented or weak field, the house name does more work.
Rule 3 — Advertising support: a new name requires advertising weight to launch and sustain it. Absent that budget, the house name is the more efficient carrier.
Rule 4 — Significance: if the product is a breakthrough that creates or redefines a category, a new name is warranted; if it is a commodity variant, use the house name.

Rule 5 — Distribution: off-the-shelf or self-serve products (including most ecommerce) rely more on the house name or descriptive naming, while products sold through reps or high-touch channels can support a distinct new name.
Tally your answers, not just one; the source presents these as a combined heuristic, and a single criterion in isolation can mislead. Then apply the naming rules for the chosen path.
caveats: These are the source's rules of thumb, not formulas with numeric thresholds; the source gives no benchmark scores or weights.
Rules interact: high volume can still be overridden by weak significance and low ad support, so use judgement.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Line-Extension Trap and Why It Dilutes the Brand
cards.summary: Extending a strong name across distinctly different products erodes the meaning of that name in the prospect's mind.
cards.use_when: Planning catalog expansion, adding a new category under an existing store brand, or evaluating a tempting free-ride addition.
steps: Identify whether the proposed addition is a close variant of what the brand already means or a distinctly different product. The source warns that the further the stretch, the more the original meaning erodes.

Apply the shopping-list test: if you named your brand and the prospect couldn't tell what category it stood for without a descriptor, the name has become too diffuse to function as a generic substitute.

Check the free-ride trap: it is tempting to attach a familiar name to a new product because recognition is already paid for, but the source argues this often costs more in lost clarity than it saves in launch spend.
Apply the teeter-totter principle: one name cannot stand for two distinctly different products without one side going down. Expect one meaning to weaken as the other is promoted.
Before committing, run the 5 rules of the road (volume, competition, ad support, significance, distribution) to decide house name vs. new name.
If you proceed, dedicate a distinct sub-brand or name for the new category rather than sharing the core brand.
caveats: The source's position is strongly anti-line-extension; modern retailers and marketplaces often extend successfully, so treat it as a warning about dilution risk rather than an absolute prohibition.
Dilution is slow and hard to measure directly; the shopping-list test is a qualitative check, not a metric.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Teeter-Totter Principle of Category Ownership
cards.summary: One brand name cannot stand for two distinctly different products without one side going down.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a store brand should own multiple categories, or during a product roadmap review before approving a stretch SKU.
steps: State what exact thing the brand stands for today in the customer's mind—usually a category, an attribute, or a price tier, not a vague 'quality' promise.
For each product the brand currently covers, score how close it is to that core meaning. The source says one name cannot stand for two distinctly different products without one meaning weakening.
When a stretch is unavoidable, plan the trade-off explicitly: accept that the original association may fade, and decide whether you are willing to pay that price.
Alternatively, segment the architecture: keep the head brand tight and give the different product its own name, so the two meanings do not compete for the same word.
Re-check the shopping-list test after each expansion—if customers can no longer use your name as a short-hand for the original category, the teeter-totter has tipped.
Document the decision so future SKU approvals stay consistent with the brand's assigned meaning.
caveats: The principle is a heuristic about perception, not a measured effect; the source offers no numeric threshold for how different is 'too different.'
Real companies do stretch brands successfully; the principle predicts pressure on meaning, not certain failure.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Shopping-List Test for a Diffuse Brand
cards.summary: If customers cannot use your brand name as a generic substitute on a shopping list, the name has become too diffuse to position.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a store brand is losing meaning, or screening a proposed extension before it further dilutes the name.
steps: Imagine a customer writing a shopping list for your category and using your brand name in place of the product noun—the way a category-defining brand becomes shorthand.
Run the test with real customers, support transcripts, or search queries: do people search your brand plus a needed category, or search the brand name expecting a specific product?
If the brand name no longer substitutes for the category noun, the source says the name has become too diffuse to function as a generic substitute.
Use the result as a gate on further extensions: a brand failing the test should not be stretched further; a brand passing it has meaning worth protecting.
Track the test over time after each launch to see whether a recent extension has hollowed out the core association.
If the test fails, choose between tightening the brand back to its core or formally splitting the architecture into distinct names.
caveats: This is a qualitative test drawn from the source, not a benchmarked metric; pass/fail depends on how customers actually talk about the category.
Brands built on lifestyle or identity, rather than category, may not be expected to substitute for a category noun; interpret the test in that light.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Bartender Test and the Limits of Brand Recall
cards.summary: Use a simple recall test to check whether a brand name evokes its category before you commit marketing spend to it.
cards.use_when: Validating a new store or product name, or measuring whether current branding has actually lodged a category association.
steps: Ask someone outside your company—the source's informal version is a bartender-style stranger—to name three brands in your category. Note whether yours appears.
Then mention your brand name and ask what it sells. If the answer is wrong or blank, the name is not yet carrying your category into the mind.
Repeat with several people who fit your avatar, since recall varies by audience and the test is only as good as the sample.
Treat a failing result as a signal to increase reinforcement (consistent name + category descriptor in every ad and PDP) rather than to blame the product.
For a new name under consideration, run the reverse: say the name and ask what category it sounds like. If listeners place it in the wrong category, expect extra teaching cost.
Track recall again after a campaign period to see whether repetition is fixing the name-category link.
caveats: The source uses an informal, illustrative test; it is not a rigorous research method and should be treated as a directional signal.
Name recall is one component of positioning; a name can recall the category yet still lose on other rungs.
